subject: math
title: Length and Perimeter
seo_title: Grade 3 Length and Perimeter Worksheets (Free, with Answer Key) | Ontario Math
standard_text: Use appropriate units of length to estimate, measure, and compare the perimeters of polygons and curved shapes, and construct polygons with a given perimeter
meta_desc: Free Grade 3 math worksheets on length and perimeter: choose mm, cm, m or km, use benchmarks, measure with a ruler even when it does not start at 0, add sides, find a missing side and solve fence and hockey rink word problems. 100 questions with an answer key, matched to the Ontario curriculum and good EQAO practice.
key_big: Start at 0, count the spaces, and add every side to find the perimeter.
key_sub: 1 cm = 10 mm, 1 m = 100 cm and 1 km = 1000 m. A rectangle has 4 sides even when only 2 numbers are shown: 8 + 3 + 8 + 3 = 22.
body_html:
Units of length

Length is how long something is. Small things use small units. Long distances use big units.

UnitBenchmark (about this long)Use it for
millimetre (mm)the thickness of a dimea ladybug, a loonie’s thickness
centimetre (cm)the width of your fingernaila pencil, a notebook
metre (m)a metre stick, or one big stepa door, a hockey rink
kilometre (km)a 15-minute walkthe Terry Fox Run, a trip to Ottawa

Key facts: 1 cm = 10 mm, 1 m = 100 cm, 1 km = 1000 m.

Measure with a ruler

Line up one end of the object with 0, not with 1 and not with the edge of the ruler. Read the number at the other end.

If the object does not start at 0, take away the start from the end, or count the spaces.

Perimeter: the distance around

Perimeter is the distance all the way around a flat shape. To find it, add every side.

For a curved side, lay a string along the edge, then measure the string with a ruler.

Fence a garden

A garden is 8 m long and 3 m wide. How much fence goes around it?

A rectangle has 4 sides, even when only 2 numbers are given: 8 + 3 + 8 + 3 = 22.

Answer: 22 m

Find a missing side

A triangle has a perimeter of 20 cm. Two sides are 6 cm and 8 cm.

Add the sides you know: 6 + 8 = 14. Subtract: 20 − 14 = 6.

Answer: 6 cm

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Starting at 1 or at the edge of the rulerStart at 0, or take away the start from the end
Counting the marks (0 to 6 is 7 marks)Count the spaces: 0 to 6 is 6 cm
Choosing km for a pencilPick a unit that fits the size: mm, cm, m or km
Adding only the two numbers shown on a rectangleAdd all 4 sides: 8 + 3 + 8 + 3
Counting the squares insideThat is the area. Perimeter counts the edges around

faq.q: What do Grade 3 students learn about length and perimeter in Ontario?
faq.a: In the Spatial Sense strand, Grade 3 students choose mm, cm, m or km, estimate with benchmarks, measure even when an object does not start at 0, and find the perimeter of polygons and curved shapes.

faq.q: What is the difference between perimeter and area?
faq.a: Perimeter is the distance around the edge of a shape, in cm or m. Area is the space inside, counted in squares. A 5 cm by 3 cm rectangle has a perimeter of 16 cm and an area of 15 square centimetres.

faq.q: How do you measure when the object does not start at 0 on the ruler?
faq.a: Subtract the start number from the end number, or count the spaces between them. A pencil from 2 cm to 9 cm is 9 − 2 = 7 cm long.

faq.q: Is perimeter on the Grade 3 EQAO math assessment?
faq.a: The Grade 3 EQAO math assessment is based on the Ontario curriculum, which includes length and perimeter, so students may see questions like these. These worksheets are good practice.

sets.title: Choose the unit and use benchmarks

items.q: Which unit is best to measure the length of a ladybug?
items.e: A ladybug is tiny, smaller than your fingernail, so use millimetres.

items.q: Which unit is best to measure the length of a crayon?
items.e: A crayon fits on a ruler, so use centimetres. Kilograms measure mass, not length.

items.q: Which unit is best to measure the length of a hockey rink?
items.e: You can skate from one end of a rink to the other in a few seconds, so use metres.

items.q: Which unit is best to measure the distance from Toronto to Ottawa?
items.e: Toronto to Ottawa is a long drive of a few hours, so use kilometres.

items.q: Which unit is best to measure how thick a loonie is?
items.e: A loonie is very thin, about 2 mm thick, so use millimetres.

items.q: Which unit is best to measure the height of the classroom door?
items.e: A door is a bit taller than an adult, about 2 m. Litres measure how much a container holds.

items.q: Which unit is best to measure the length of the Terry Fox Run route?
items.e: The Terry Fox Run is a long walk or run, so use kilometres.

items.q: Which unit is best to measure the width of your math notebook?
items.e: A notebook fits on your desk and on a 30 cm ruler, so use centimetres.

items.q: How many millimetres are in 1 centimetre?
items.e: Look at a ruler. There are 10 small spaces in each centimetre. So 1 cm = 10 mm.

items.q: How many centimetres are in 1 metre?
items.e: A metre stick has 100 centimetres marked on it. So 1 m = 100 cm.

items.q: How many metres are in 1 kilometre?
items.e: Kilo means 1000. So 1 km = 1000 m.

items.q: Which list goes from the shortest unit to the longest unit?
items.e: A millimetre is the smallest. 10 mm make 1 cm, 100 cm make 1 m, and 1000 m make 1 km.

items.q: Choose the best estimate. Your fingernail is about ☐ wide.
items.e: The width of a fingernail is a good benchmark for 1 cm. 1 mm is about as thick as a dime.

items.q: Choose the best estimate. A dime is about ☐ thick.
items.e: A dime is very thin. Its thickness is a good benchmark for 1 mm.

items.q: Choose the best estimate. A classroom door is about ☐ tall.
items.e: A door is a bit taller than an adult. That is about 2 m. 2 cm is shorter than your finger.

items.q: Choose the best estimate. A new pencil is about ☐ long.
items.e: A new pencil fits on a 30 cm ruler, so it is about 19 cm. 19 mm is only about as long as a fingertip.

items.q: Choose the best estimate. A Grade 3 student is about ☐ tall.
items.e: Most Grade 3 students are between 1 m and 1 m 50 cm tall. 130 cm fits. 13 cm is the size of a hand.

items.q: Choose the best estimate. A school bus is about ☐ long.
items.e: A school bus is about as long as 6 classroom doors lying end to end, so about 12 m.

items.q: Choose the best estimate. You can walk about ☐ in 15 minutes.
items.e: A 15-minute walk is a good benchmark for 1 km. You can walk 1 m in one big step.

items.q: Which is about 1 m long?
c: a metre stick, or a big step
items.e: 1 m is the length of a metre stick, or about one big step for an adult. A fingernail is about 1 cm.

sets.title: Measure with a ruler (not always from 0)

items.e: The pencil starts at 0 and ends at 7. So it is 7 cm long. Count the spaces between the numbers, not the marks: there are 8 marks but only 7 spaces.
The crayon starts at 0 and ends at 5. So it is 5 cm long. Count the spaces between the numbers, not the marks: there are 6 marks but only 5 spaces.
The eraser starts at 0 and ends at 4. So it is 4 cm long. Count the spaces between the numbers, not the marks: there are 5 marks but only 4 spaces.
The piece of ribbon starts at 0 and ends at 9. So it is 9 cm long. Count the spaces between the numbers, not the marks: there are 10 marks but only 9 spaces.
The pencil starts at 2, not at 0. It ends at 9. 9 − 2 = 7, so it is 7 cm long. You can also count the spaces from 2 to 9: there are 7.
The crayon starts at 1, not at 0. It ends at 6. 6 − 1 = 5, so it is 5 cm long. You can also count the spaces from 1 to 6: there are 5.
The eraser starts at 3, not at 0. It ends at 7. 7 − 3 = 4, so it is 4 cm long. You can also count the spaces from 3 to 7: there are 4.
The piece of ribbon starts at 2, not at 0. It ends at 8. 8 − 2 = 6, so it is 6 cm long. You can also count the spaces from 2 to 8: there are 6.
The pencil starts at 3, not at 0. It ends at 11. 11 − 3 = 8, so it is 8 cm long. You can also count the spaces from 3 to 11: there are 8.
The toy hockey stick starts at 4, not at 0. It ends at 9. 9 − 4 = 5, so it is 5 cm long. You can also count the spaces from 4 to 9: there are 5.

items.q: Owen puts one end of his crayon at 1 on the ruler, not at 0. The other end is at 8. How long is it?
items.e: He started at 1, so the number at the end is 1 too big. 8 − 1 = 7 cm.

items.q: Hana puts one end of her library card at 1 on the ruler, not at 0. The other end is at 10. How long is it?
items.e: She started at 1, so the number at the end is 1 too big. 10 − 1 = 9 cm.
The crayon goes past 4 cm and then 6 small marks more. 4 cm = 40 mm, and 40 + 6 = 46. So it is 46 mm long.
The pencil goes past 6 cm and then 3 small marks more. 6 cm = 60 mm, and 60 + 3 = 63. So it is 63 mm long.
The eraser goes past 3 cm and then 5 small marks more. 3 cm = 30 mm, and 30 + 5 = 35. So it is 35 mm long.
The pencil starts at 2 cm, not at 0. It ends at 7 cm and 4 small marks, which is 74 mm. 2 cm = 20 mm. 74 − 20 = 54 mm.
The crayon starts at 3 cm = 30 mm. It ends at 8 cm and 8 small marks, which is 88 mm. 88 − 30 = 58 mm.

items.q: Leah measures a ribbon. It goes from 0 to 6 on the ruler. She counts the marks 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and says the ribbon is 7 cm. How long is it really?
items.e: Leah counted 7 marks, but length is the number of spaces between them. From 0 to 6 there are 6 spaces, so the ribbon is 6 cm.

items.q: Sofia’s marker lies on a ruler. One end is at the 4 cm mark and the other end is at the 12 cm mark. How long is the marker?
items.e: It does not start at 0, so subtract: 12 − 4 = 8 cm. 16 cm adds the numbers instead.

items.q: A paper clip is 30 mm long. How many centimetres is that?
items.e: 10 mm = 1 cm. 30 mm is 3 groups of 10 mm, so it is 3 cm.

items.q: Each small square is 1 cm on each side. What is the perimeter of the rectangle?
items.e: Count the 1 cm sides all the way around: 4 + 2 + 4 + 2 = 12 cm. 8 is the number of squares inside. That is the area, not the perimeter.

items.q: Each small square is 1 cm on each side. What is the perimeter of the rectangle?
items.e: Count the 1 cm sides all the way around: 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16 cm. 15 is the number of squares inside. That is the area, not the perimeter.

items.q: Each small square is 1 cm on each side. What is the perimeter of the square?
items.e: Count the 1 cm sides all the way around: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12 cm. 9 is the number of squares inside. That is the area, not the perimeter.

items.q: Each small square is 1 cm on each side. What is the perimeter of the rectangle?
items.e: Count the 1 cm sides all the way around: 6 + 2 + 6 + 2 = 16 cm. 12 is the number of squares inside. That is the area, not the perimeter.

items.q: Each small square is 1 cm on each side. What is the perimeter of the rectangle?
items.e: Count the 1 cm sides all the way around: 2 + 5 + 2 + 5 = 14 cm. 10 is the number of squares inside. That is the area, not the perimeter.

items.q: Each small square is 1 cm on each side. What is the perimeter of the shape?
items.e: Go around the outside and count every 1 cm side, including the short step: 18 cm. There are 14 squares inside, but that is the area.

items.q: What is the perimeter of this triangle?
items.e: Add every side: 4 + 11 + 12 = 27 cm. Touch each side as you add it so you do not skip one.

items.q: What is the perimeter of this triangle?
items.e: Add every side: 5 + 4 + 6 = 15 m. Touch each side as you add it so you do not skip one.

items.q: What is the perimeter of this quadrilateral?
items.e: Add every side: 6 + 5 + 7 + 4 = 22 cm. Touch each side as you add it so you do not skip one.

items.q: What is the perimeter of this quadrilateral?
items.e: Add every side: 12 + 10 + 15 + 9 = 46 m. Touch each side as you add it so you do not skip one.

items.q: What is the perimeter of this pentagon?
items.e: Add every side: 7 + 7 + 7 + 10 + 5 = 36 cm. Touch each side as you add it so you do not skip one.

items.q: What is the perimeter of this pentagon?
items.e: Add every side: 3 + 3 + 3 + 6 + 3 = 18 m. Touch each side as you add it so you do not skip one.

items.q: What is the perimeter of the rectangle?
items.e: A rectangle has 2 long sides and 2 short sides: 9 + 4 + 9 + 4 = 26 cm. Adding only 9 + 4 = 13 forgets the other two sides.

items.q: What is the perimeter of the rectangle?
items.e: A rectangle has 2 long sides and 2 short sides: 12 + 5 + 12 + 5 = 34 m. Adding only 12 + 5 = 17 forgets the other two sides.

items.q: This is a square. What is its perimeter?
items.e: A square has 4 equal sides: 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 24 cm.

items.q: This is a square. What is its perimeter?
items.e: A square has 4 equal sides: 8 + 8 + 8 + 8 = 32 m.

items.q: All the sides of this hexagon are the same length. What is its perimeter?
items.e: A hexagon has 6 sides. Add 5 cm 6 times: 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 30 cm.

items.q: All the sides of this octagon are the same length. What is its perimeter?
items.e: An octagon has 8 sides. Add 3 cm 8 times: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 24 cm.

items.q: How can you measure the perimeter of a shape with a curved side?
c: Count the squares inside the shape
Measure across the middle of the shape
Lay a string along the edge, then measure the string
items.e: A ruler cannot bend around a curve. Lay a string all the way around the edge, mark where it meets, then straighten the string and measure it with a ruler.

items.q: What is perimeter?
c: the distance all the way around a shape
the length of the longest side
items.e: Perimeter is the distance around the outside edge. The space inside is the area.

sets.title: Find the missing side and build a shape

items.q: The perimeter of this triangle is 35 cm. What is the missing side length?
items.e: Add the sides you know: 12 + 14 = 26. Then subtract from the perimeter: 35 − 26 = 9 cm.

items.q: The perimeter of this quadrilateral is 51 m. What is the missing side length?
items.e: Add the sides you know: 13 + 12 + 12 = 37. Then subtract from the perimeter: 51 − 37 = 14 m.

items.q: The perimeter of this triangle is 26 cm. What is the missing side length?
items.e: Add the sides you know: 6 + 8 = 14. Then subtract from the perimeter: 26 − 14 = 12 cm.

items.q: The perimeter of this quadrilateral is 47 m. What is the missing side length?
items.e: Add the sides you know: 12 + 11 + 13 = 36. Then subtract from the perimeter: 47 − 36 = 11 m.

items.q: The perimeter of this triangle is 32 cm. What is the missing side length?
items.e: Add the sides you know: 11 + 6 = 17. Then subtract from the perimeter: 32 − 17 = 15 cm.

items.q: The perimeter of this quadrilateral is 25 m. What is the missing side length?
items.e: Add the sides you know: 5 + 8 + 5 = 18. Then subtract from the perimeter: 25 − 18 = 7 m.

items.q: The perimeter of this triangle is 19 cm. What is the missing side length?
items.e: Add the sides you know: 6 + 8 = 14. Then subtract from the perimeter: 19 − 14 = 5 cm.

items.q: The perimeter of this quadrilateral is 29 m. What is the missing side length?
items.e: Add the sides you know: 7 + 7 + 8 = 22. Then subtract from the perimeter: 29 − 22 = 7 m.

items.q: A rectangle has a perimeter of 22 cm. It is 8 cm long. How wide is it?
items.e: The two lengths use 8 + 8 = 16 cm. That leaves 22 − 16 = 6 cm for the two widths, so each width is 6 ÷ 2 = 3 cm.

items.q: A rectangle has a perimeter of 32 m. It is 10 m long. How wide is it?
items.e: The two lengths use 10 + 10 = 20 m. That leaves 32 − 20 = 12 m for the two widths, so each width is 12 ÷ 2 = 6 m.

items.q: A rectangle has a perimeter of 24 cm. It is 7 cm long. How wide is it?
items.e: The two lengths use 7 + 7 = 14 cm. That leaves 24 − 14 = 10 cm for the two widths, so each width is 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm.

items.q: A rectangle has a perimeter of 32 m. It is 12 m long. How wide is it?
items.e: The two lengths use 12 + 12 = 24 m. That leaves 32 − 24 = 8 m for the two widths, so each width is 8 ÷ 2 = 4 m.

items.q: A rectangle has a perimeter of 22 cm. It is 9 cm long. How wide is it?
items.e: The two lengths use 9 + 9 = 18 cm. That leaves 22 − 18 = 4 cm for the two widths, so each width is 4 ÷ 2 = 2 cm.

items.q: A square has a perimeter of 20 cm. How long is each side?
items.e: A square has 4 equal sides. 20 ÷ 4 = 5 cm. Check: 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20.

items.q: A square has a perimeter of 36 m. How long is each side?
items.e: A square has 4 equal sides. 36 ÷ 4 = 9 m. Check: 9 + 9 + 9 + 9 = 36.

items.q: A square has a perimeter of 28 cm. How long is each side?
items.e: A square has 4 equal sides. 28 ÷ 4 = 7 cm. Check: 7 + 7 + 7 + 7 = 28.

items.q: Which rectangle has a perimeter of 20 cm?
items.e: 6 + 4 + 6 + 4 = 20 cm. A quick check: length + width must be half of 20, which is 10. 4 cm by 5 cm has an area of 20, not a perimeter of 20.

items.q: Which rectangle has a perimeter of 16 cm?
items.e: 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16 cm. A quick check: length + width must be half of 16, which is 8. 2 cm by 8 cm has an area of 16, not a perimeter of 16.

items.q: Which rectangle has a perimeter of 24 cm?
items.e: 8 + 4 + 8 + 4 = 24 cm. A quick check: length + width must be half of 24, which is 12. 4 cm by 6 cm has an area of 24, not a perimeter of 24.

items.q: Which rectangle has a perimeter of 18 cm?
items.e: 7 + 2 + 7 + 2 = 18 cm. A quick check: length + width must be half of 18, which is 9. 2 cm by 9 cm has an area of 18, not a perimeter of 18.

sets.title: Word problems: fences, rinks and runs

items.q: Priya’s family has a vegetable garden that is 8 m long and 5 m wide. They want a fence all the way around it. How much fence do they need?
items.e: The fence goes around all 4 sides: 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26 m. 40 is the area, and 13 m is only two sides.

items.q: A hockey rink is about 60 m long and 30 m wide. About how far is it all the way around the boards?
items.e: Add all 4 sides: 60 + 30 + 60 + 30 = 180 m. 90 m is only one length and one width.

items.q: For the Terry Fox Run, Grade 3 runs around the school field. The field is 150 m long and 100 m wide. How far is one lap?
items.e: One lap goes around all 4 sides: 150 + 100 + 150 + 100 = 500 m. 400 m leaves out one short side.

items.q: One lap around that field is 500 m. How many laps make 1 km?
items.e: 1 km = 1000 m. 500 m + 500 m = 1000 m, so 2 laps make 1 km.

items.q: Zoe glues ribbon around the edge of a square picture frame. Each side is 25 cm. How much ribbon does she need?
items.e: A square has 4 equal sides: 25 + 25 + 25 + 25 = 100 cm. 75 cm forgets one side.

items.q: The class bulletin board is 120 cm long and 90 cm wide. Mr. Singh puts a paper border around it. How long is the border?
items.e: Add all 4 sides: 120 + 90 + 120 + 90 = 420 cm. 210 cm is only one length and one width.

items.q: A park is shaped like a triangle. Its sides are 120 m, 150 m and 90 m. Arjun walks once around the park. How far does he walk?
items.e: Add the 3 sides: 120 + 150 + 90 = 360 m.

items.q: Liam’s family makes a backyard skating rink that is 10 m long and 6 m wide. They put boards around all the edges. How many metres of boards do they need?
items.e: Boards go around all 4 sides: 10 + 6 + 10 + 6 = 32 m. 60 would be the area of the rink.

items.q: A dog pen is 9 m long and 4 m wide. One long side is the wall of the house, so it needs no fence. How much fence is needed for the other 3 sides?
items.e: Only 3 sides get fence: 4 + 9 + 4 = 17 m. 26 m would put fence along the house wall too.

items.q: Kai’s family paddles their canoe 3 km to an island and 3 km back to the cottage. How far do they paddle?
items.e: There and back is 3 km + 3 km = 6 km.

items.q: The CN Tower in Toronto is 553 m tall. How much less than 1 km is that?
A ladybug is 7 mm long. A beetle is 3 cm long. How much longer is the beetle?
items.e: Change to the same unit first: 3 cm = 30 mm. 30 − 7 = 23 mm. Do not take 3 from 7.

items.q: Ethan used 30 m of fence to go around a rectangular garden. The garden is 9 m long. How wide is it?
items.e: Two lengths: 9 + 9 = 18 m. 30 − 18 = 12 m for the two widths. 12 ÷ 2 = 6 m.

items.q: A square sandbox has a perimeter of 12 m. How long is each side?
items.e: A square has 4 equal sides. 12 ÷ 4 = 3 m. Check: 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12.

items.q: Garden A is 8 m by 2 m. Garden B is 5 m by 5 m. Which garden needs more fence to go around it?
items.e: A: 8 + 2 + 8 + 2 = 20 m. B: 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20 m. They need the same fence. B has more space inside (25 is its area), but the same perimeter.

items.q: A rug is 3 m long and 2 m wide. Ava sews a strip of trim around all the edges. How much trim does she use?
items.e: Perimeter = 3 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 10 m. 6 is the area of the rug, and 5 m is only two sides.

items.q: Maya wants to put tape around the edge of a table that is 90 cm long and 60 cm wide. She has 250 cm of tape. Is that enough?
items.e: Perimeter = 90 + 60 + 90 + 60 = 300 cm. 300 cm is more than 250 cm, so it is not enough. 150 cm is only one length and one width.

items.q: Mei cuts out a sign shaped like a hexagon. All 6 sides are 15 cm long. She puts gold ribbon around the edge. How much ribbon does she use?
items.e: 6 sides of 15 cm: 15 + 15 + 15 + 15 + 15 + 15 = 90 cm. 75 cm leaves out one side.

items.q: A soccer field at the park is 100 m long and 60 m wide. Owen jogs once around it. How far does he jog?
items.e: Add all 4 sides: 100 + 60 + 100 + 60 = 320 m. 160 m is only half of the way around.

items.q: Noah has 85 cm of ribbon. He cuts off 30 cm to wrap a gift. How much ribbon is left?
items.e: Cutting off means subtract: 85 − 30 = 55 cm.
